title: read() the whole file
blurb: open() in 'r' mode gives a file handle with the pointer at 0; read() returns everything and leaves the pointer at the end.

setup.MyData.txt:
This is  a test file
it is stored in hard disk

notes.1: open() finds MyData.txt and returns a file handle (a TextIOWrapper). The pointer starts at position 0 – the T.
notes.2: read() with no size reads from the pointer to the end of the file: all 46 characters, including the \n between the lines. The pointer is now at 46 (end of file).
notes.3: print() shows the string. The \n inside it makes the second line appear on its own row.
notes.4: close() releases the file. The handle shows closed = True. The text in str1 stays – it is a normal string in memory now.

title: read(n) moves the file pointer
blurb: read(6) returns 6 characters and moves the pointer 6 places; the next read(10) continues from there.

setup.MyData.txt:
This is  a test file
it is stored in hard disk

notes.1: The pointer starts at 0, in front of the T.
notes.2: read(6) takes 6 characters: T h i s ␠ i. The pointer moves to 6, in front of the s.
notes.4: read(10) continues from 6, not from 0: s ␠ ␠ a ␠ t e s t ␠. The pointer moves to 16.
notes.5: Prints s  a test  – the read started where the previous one stopped.
notes.6: tell() reports the pointer: 16. It is the number of characters already consumed.

title: Using a file after close()
blurb: close() releases the file. The handle object still exists (name, mode work) but any I/O on it raises ValueError.

setup.MyData.txt:
apples are red
grapes are green

notes.3: The handle object still exists – its attributes still work: name.
notes.6: Any I/O on a closed file raises ValueError: I/O operation on closed file.

title: with closes the file for you
blurb: The with statement calls close() automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens inside it.

notes.1: with ... as file: opens the file and binds the handle to file.
notes.2: writelines() writes each string of the list as is – it does NOT add newlines, so each item carries its own \n. Buffered.
notes.3: Inside the block the file is open: False.
notes.4: Leaving the block runs the with line again to exit: close() is called automatically and the buffer is flushed to disk.
notes.6: Read it back with a new handle: both lines are there.

title: 'w' mode overwrites
blurb: From overwrittingFile.py: every open(..., 'w') wipes the file first, so only the last version survives.

notes.1: 'w' creates overwrite.txt (it did not exist) and the file is empty – 0 bytes.
notes.2: write() returns 17 and moves the pointer to 17, but the text is still in Python's write buffer – the file on disk is still empty.
notes.3: close() flushes the buffer to disk. Now the file holds Writing Version 0.
notes.4: Opening the SAME file again with 'w' wipes it instantly – the old text is gone before anything is written.
notes.5: Version 1 goes into the buffer (pointer 17); disk still empty.
notes.6: close() flushes: the file now holds only Writing Version 1.
notes.7: Reopen in 'r' to check what survived. Pointer at 0.
notes.8: Prints Writing Version 1 – the comment in overwrittingFile.py is right.

title: 'a' mode appends
blurb: From appendFile.py: 'a' creates the file if needed and always writes at the end, so both versions stay.

notes.1: 'a' creates append.txt because it does not exist (append mode does NOT need the file to exist). Pointer at 0 of an empty file.
notes.2: Version 0 goes into the buffer; pointer 17.
notes.3: close() flushes – the file holds Writing Version 0.
notes.4: Opening with 'a' keeps the content and puts the pointer at the END (17).
notes.5: Version 1 is buffered after the existing text; pointer 34.
notes.6: close() flushes – both versions are on disk, with no newline between them because none was written.
notes.8: Prints Writing Version 0Writing Version 1. Run appendFile.py again and the text grows again – append never wipes.

title: 'x' mode: new files only
blurb: From writingToNewFileOnly.py: 'x' creates and writes a brand-new file, and raises FileExistsError if the file is already there.

notes.1: 'x' = exclusive creation. newWrite.txt does not exist, so Python creates it.
notes.2: Write into the buffer – pointer 17, disk still empty.
notes.3: close() flushes – newWrite.txt now holds Writing Version 2.
notes.4: overwrite.txt already exists, so 'x' refuses to open it. Nothing is created or wiped and the line raises FileExistsError – exactly what writingToNewFileOnly.py logs.

title: 'r+' read then write
blurb: From readWriteFile.py: r+ keeps the content; after read() the pointer is at the end, so write() adds 123 after ABCDEF.

notes.1: 'r+' opens an EXISTING file for reading and writing. Nothing is wiped; pointer at 0.
notes.2: read() consumes everything – the pointer is now at 6, after the F.
notes.4: write() writes at the pointer, which is at the end, so 123 goes after ABCDEF (buffered for now).
notes.5: close() flushes – the file holds ABCDEF123, as the comment in readWriteFile.py says.

title: 'w+' write then read
blurb: From readWriteFile.py: w+ wipes the file on open; after write() the pointer is past the new text, so read() returns '' until you seek(0).

notes.1: 'w+' wipes the file the moment it opens – ABCDEF123 is gone. Pointer at 0.
notes.2: 789 is written into the buffer; the pointer moves to 3.
notes.3: read() reads from the pointer, which is already at 3 = end of file, so it returns ''. (read() also flushes the pending write, so 789 is now on disk.)
notes.4: Prints '' – empty, even though the file holds 789.
notes.5: seek(0, 0) moves the pointer back to the start (offset 0, from the beginning).

title: 'w+' read first = empty
blurb: fun_WriteAndReadInDifferentOrder from readWriteFile.py: the wipe happens inside open(), before read() runs.

notes.1: 'w+' wipes the file inside open() – 789 is gone before any other line runs.
notes.2: read() on an empty file returns ''.
notes.3: Prints '' – this is the blank output explained in the comments of readWriteFile.py.

title: 'a+' append and read
blurb: a+ starts with the pointer at the END, so read() is empty until you seek(0); write() always goes to the end.

notes.1: 'a+' keeps the content and starts with the pointer at the END (8).
notes.3: read() from the end returns '' – a common surprise with a+.
notes.4: seek(0) moves to the start so reading works.
notes.5: Prints 10 11 12; the pointer is back at the end.
notes.6: In append mode every write goes to the end, wherever the pointer is.

title: readline() vs readlines()
blurb: readline() returns one line including its \n; readlines() returns the remaining lines as a list; at the end of file you get '' or [].

setup.MyData.txt:
apples are red
grapes are green

notes.2: readline() reads up to and including the first \n: 'apples are red\n'. The pointer moves to 15 (start of line 2).
notes.3: end='' stops print() adding a second newline – the line already ends with \n. Without it you get a blank line between the lines (the PDF output).
notes.4: The next readline() continues from 15 and returns 'grapes are green\n'. Pointer at 32 = end of file.
notes.6: At the end of the file readline() returns an empty string '' – that is how you detect EOF.
notes.7: seek(0) moves the pointer back to the start so the file can be read again.
notes.8: readlines() reads every remaining line into a list of strings, each keeping its \n.
notes.10: closed is a property (no brackets) – True after close().

title: write() is buffered until flush()
blurb: write() first lands in a memory buffer. flush() pushes it to the disk; close() flushes too. Watch the file on disk stay empty.

notes.2: write() puts the text in a memory buffer; disk still empty.
notes.3: flush() pushes the buffer to disk now, without closing.
notes.4: The second line is buffered again.
notes.5: A second reader sees only what was flushed: python is simple.
notes.6: close() flushes the rest and releases the file.
notes.7: Now both lines are on disk.

title: seek() and tell() on a binary file
blurb: The fileOperation.ipynb walk-through on test.txt (ABCDEFGHIJ): whence 0 = from start, 1 = from current, 2 = from end.

notes.1: 'rb' opens test.txt as raw bytes. Pointer at 0 (A).
notes.2: read(2) returns bytes b'AB' – the b prefix means bytes, not str. Pointer 2.
notes.4: seek(4, 0): 4 bytes from the BEGINNING → pointer at 4 (E).
notes.6: seek(2, 1): 2 bytes forward from the CURRENT position 6 → 8 (I).
notes.9: seek(-8, 1): 8 bytes BACK from the current position 9 → 1 (B). Negative offsets are allowed in binary mode.
notes.11: seek(-2, 2): 2 bytes back from the END (10) → 8 (I).
notes.12: read(2) → b'IJ'. Pointer 10 = end of file.

title: Text mode cannot seek from current
blurb: Relative seeks (whence 1 or 2 with a non-zero offset) only work in binary mode. In text mode Python refuses.

notes.1: Same file, but opened in TEXT mode 'r'.
notes.2: read(2) → 'AB' (a str this time, no b prefix).
notes.3: In text mode only seek(n, 0) and seek(0, 1) / seek(0, 2) are allowed. A non-zero offset from the current position raises io.UnsupportedOperation. Open the file with 'rb' for relative seeks.

title: Fixed-size records with struct
blurb: binaryOperations.py, flattened: each player is packed into 14 bytes ('i10s'), so record N starts at byte N*14.

notes.1: struct converts Python values to fixed-size bytes.
notes.3: pack('i10s', 14, b'Smith     ') → 4 bytes for the int 14 (0e 00 00 00, little-endian) + 10 bytes for the name = 14 bytes. In the buffer, not yet on disk.
notes.6: close() flushes all 42 bytes. Every record is exactly 14 bytes, which is what makes random access possible.
notes.7: Open the same file for reading bytes.
notes.8: Record index 2 starts at 2 × 14 = 28 – jump straight there with seek, no need to read records 0 and 1.
notes.10: unpack('i10s', ...) turns the 14 bytes back into (7, b'Dhoni     ').
notes.11: Prints Id: 7, Name : Dhoni (the name keeps its padding spaces – .strip() would remove them).

title: pickle.dump and pickle.load
blurb: Student objects are turned into bytes with dump() (binary mode) and rebuilt with load(), one object per call.

notes.1: pickle serialises Python objects to bytes.
notes.2: Student lives in its own file (Student.py) and is imported, as in the PDF.
notes.3: Two Student objects in a list.
notes.4: Pickling must use a BINARY mode ('wb') – pickle writes bytes.
notes.5: dump() converts studs[0] into 69 bytes (class name + attributes) and writes them. Buffered for now.
notes.7: close() flushes: students.data holds both objects back-to-back. 80 04 95 is the pickle header (protocol 4).
notes.9: load() reads exactly ONE object and rebuilds it: Student(roll=10, name='John', dept='cs'). Pointer 69.
notes.10: display() is a normal method of the rebuilt object.
notes.11: The next load() returns the second object. Pointer 138 = end.
notes.13: There is no third object. load() at the end of the file raises EOFError: Ran out of input – that is why the PDF loops exactly range(3) for 3 objects.
